chunks: "I'd say the premise is slightly off in two ways. First, many turns of thin wire doesn't mean lots of current; it means the opposite.
Force depends on ampere-turns, so if I use ten times as many turns I need only a tenth of the current.
More turns of thinner wire has higher resistance, and at a given supply voltage it draws less current.
A designer chooses the number of turns so that the current at the rated voltage suits the wire: for instance 4500 turns of about 0.
12 mm wire draws 45 milliamps at 12 volts and makes the same ampere-turns as 1900 turns drawing 107 milliamps on 5 volts.
Second, the large currents only happen in specific situations: the instant of start when back-EMF is zero, a stall, or overload.
A running motor draws much less than V over R because the back-EMF opposes the supply. A solenoid is rated for a duty cycle because it draws V over R continuously and heats.
So do coils always burn out? No. They fail when heat gets ahead of cooling: stall, too much voltage, too much duty, poor ventilation, high ambient.
The wire survives because the design keeps current density to a few amps per square millimetre in continuous duty and the coil has the thermal mass and cooling to carry the heat away.
Beyond that, a coil is a thermal clock: at 20 amps/mm² it heats at about 2 K per second, so it can tolerate a short pulse but not a stall."
